ANNUAL MEETING. 


The Fifty-first Annual Meeting of the Young Men’s 
Christian Association was held on Tuesday evening, May 
15th, at 8.15 o’clock, in the Lecture Hall. 

Mr. C. T. Williams, the President, occupied the chair. 
The Chairman read a portion of the 119th Psalm, and the 
Rey. J. L. Gilmour, Pastor of Olivet Baptist Church, 
offered prayer. 

On the platform were seated representatives of the 
different Committees. The Secretary read the minutes of 
the previous Annual Meeting which were confirmed. 

The President explained that the Board of Directors had 
decided to change the form of the Annual Meeting, and 
asked each Chairman of Committees or Departments, to 
present an outline of the work of the year in five minutes, 
reserving the report of the Board of Directors to the end. 
He then introduced the men as follows : 


Membership G24 3.065 on: ¥ ke BS Shaw. 

(In the absence of the Chairman, Mr. C. T, Hare.) 
Phyisical). sci. st apaan oe Oy ebolend, 
SOcIatE- Gs acer tes ok. « -Alee Arthur.

VAM PO Rd eo oe kolymants” «ieinureleae W. H. Blackaller.

L. H. Packard. 
Report of Directors .......D. A. Budge. 


On motion of R. H. Buchanan, seconded by R. L. 
Charlton, the above reports were received and adopted, 
and ordered to be printed as the Annual Report of the 
Association, for distribution amongst members and sub- 
scribers. 

Mr. 8. P. Leet, Chairman of the Committee on Vacan- 


8 


cies, presented the following nominations to replace the 
Directors who retired this year: 


John Kennedy, R. H. Buchanan, ©. C. Holland, 
Chas. Cushing, Robt. Munro, W. M. Birks. 


R. L. Charlton, 


As no other nominations were presented, these gentlemen 
were elected by ballot to serve as Dirctors for the next 
three years. 

A vote of thanks was extended to the press, the 
members of the various Committees, and the Ladies’ Com- 
mittee, for the helpful service they had rendered in the 
prosecution of the Association work during the year. 

Mr. L. H. Packard, on behalf of the Association, referred 
to the great indebtedness all the members felt on account 
of the efficient service which had been rendered by our 
retiring President, Mr. Chas. T. Williams, who had so 
faithfully served the Association and its immediate needs 
for the past four years. 

The Chairman then introduced Mr. C. C. Michener, Field 
Secretary of the International Committee, New York, 
who gave a thirty minute address on ne w features in the 
Association movement, both at home and abroad. 

The meeting then adjourned.

Gifts towards the annual expenses of the Association, and also 
towards its extension in the city, are earnestly solicited by the 
Board of Directors. 

The Association appeals to its many friends in the city, for a re- 
membrance in the final disposition of their property. Gifts are 
invited toward an Annex to the present Building for the enlarge- 
ment of the Physical and Educational work, and, also, for special 
accommodation for work for boys; also Branch Building at Point St. 
Charles, (see Directors’ report, pages 17-19); also for the develop- 
ment of the Library, and the supervision of the Educational work. 


ANNUAL REPORT OF BOARD OF DIRECTORS. 


Jubilee Year. 


The past year has been one of exceptional interest to 
the young men of this continent. It marked the Fiftieth 
Anniversary of the founding of the Young Men’s Christian 
Association in America. Montreal was honored as the 
birthplace of the movement. On June 8-10, a series of 
meetings celebrating this important event were held. 
Representatives from the following countries took part: 
England, Ireland, Scotland, the United States, France, 
Switzerland, Germany and Belgium. These memorable 
addresses, delivered by Lord Kinnaird, Messrs. John 
R. Mott, Howard Williams, W. M. Oatts, Dr. Lucien C. 
Warner, and others, have been published. It was an occa- 
sion full of inspiration. 

Then followed the great Jubilee demonstration in 
Boston, attended by over three thousand delegates from 
all sections of this country and from foreign lands. 
Thanksgiving to God was offered for a half century of 
work for and in behalf of young men. The effect of this 
gathering upon the future of the movement cannot be 
estimated. 

The greatest discovery of the past twenty-five years has 
been the value and importance of young men. More 
attention is now paid to their education, as they have 
shown themselves more powerful and effective in business 
and professional life. There is no greater interest in all 
the world than that of young men grouped together, 
especially with some high ideal. This is one reason why 
the Young Men’s Christian Association has attracted such 
attention, and why its growth has been so phenomenal. 
Last year on this continent fifty Buildings were erected, 
an average of one each week, and ten million dollars sub- 
scribed to the different branches of the work. Its growth 


17 


has not only been due to its adaptability to the needs of 
all classes and conditions of men at home and abroad, but 
to the fact that it has a positive religious basis for its 
work, which distinguishes it from the many good but 
purely humanitarian agencies. Who can prophesy what 
the result will be in the next twenty-five years? 


Visits of Men. 


In addition to the above distinguished visitors, the mem- 
bers have been privileged in hearing Association leaders 
from other sections. Messrs. E. L. Shuey, of Dayton, 
Ohio, and Geo. B. Hodge, of New York, in their conference 
with the manufacturers as also with the members, render- 
ed valuable service on the line of educational work and 
its possibilities. Mr. F. 8S. Goodman, of New York, 
rendered similar service in the development of the Religi- 
ous Work and Bible Study. Mr. John R. Mott’s Conference 
on the Foreign Work and its outlook was most inspiring, 
and Mr. E. M. Robinson’s presentation of the future of 
this work for Boys was both helpful and suggestive. By 
the visits of these experienced men the Directors have 
sought to educate the rank and file of the members on the 
growing work of the Association. 


Membership. 


We began the year with 2,070 young men and boys 
enrolled as members. We close the year with 2,115. No 
name is counted unless the annual dues are paid in 
advance. $8,582.00 has been received from members’ 
fees. In 1897-98, the reecipts from membership fees were 
$6,146; in 1898-99, $6,223; in 1899-00, $6,660; in 1900-01, 
&8,164; and in 1901-02, $8,582. The Directors hope to see 
the receipts from members’ fees reach $10,000. 


Cost of Membership. 


It is apparent to all that the privileges here offered 
could not be provided from the sum received from mem- 


18 


bers’ fees. That sum is about one-half the amount requir- 
ed to conduct the Association. No Young Men’s Christian 
Association in the country is self-supporting. If it were 
it would only be aclub. This would render it independent 
of deserved criticism, and it would soon pass from that 
Christian control to which it owes its abundant useful- 
ness. As this fact concerning the cost of membership 
becomes known the Directors are sure that there will be 
an increasing number who will gladly add to their fee an 
annual gift toward the support of the work. And here 
the Directors wish to thank the members for their 
generous response to the recent financial appeal. $1,775 
was received, which has been a great stimulus to the 
efforts of the Finance Committee. 


The Finances. 


The Directors are grateful to be able to report that 
over $3,000 of unusual expense has been met in addition 
to the current work, and all bills have been paid. They 
wish to thank the citizens as well as the members for 
the financial help so cheerfully rendered. 


Branches. 


We had expected to be able to report the Railroad 
Branch Building as completed, but delays over which we 
had no control, have prevented. These now seem to have 
been providential. A new site has been selected, and the 
architects are now completing plans for the same. Last 
year subscriptions amounting to over $11,000 were secured, 
and this will be added to the appropriation offered by the 
Grand Trunk Railway authorities. 

The question of a Branch in the north-east end of the 
city is also under consideration. 


The Young Men on Committees. 


The young men on the various Committees, on whom 
the responsibility for the work has been placed, have 
rendered noble service. The Directors wish to record 


19 


their appreciation of the sacrifice of time and effort which 
has been so freely given. They also recognize the splendid 
training which this Committee work affords, and in view 
of this fact, their policy for the future will be so to plan 
the work that the largest possible number of members 
may be enlisted on the various Committees, and those who 
may not be able to serve on organized committees may be 
secured to render independent service in other ways. In 
all Departments we have had twenty-three Committees, 
with a total membership of 170. The future history of 
the Association work in this city is now in the hands of the 
boys and young men who have the privilege of this unique 
Training School, and who are rendering this unselfish, 
voluntary service on behalf of their fellow young men. 


The Social Llfe of Men. 


That it is most important to maintain attractive, 
healthy, social centres, with elevated purpose, for young 
men, in large cities, must be admitted. Companions will 
be found somewhere, and the companionship of a young 
man’s leisure time either makes or mars his life. The 
Directors are pleased to note that the report of this Com- 
mittee shows that a distinct gain has been made. The 
division of members into groups for social evenings has 
been more helpful than the former crowded social recep- 
tions. The various clubs have largely added to the Social 
life of the Building and should be encouraged. The fact, 
however, that a genuine social spirit has not been confined 
to stated social functions, but has been developed in all 
departments, by means of banquets, teas, and informal 
gatherings, has been most satisfactory. The change from 
the Strangers’ Tea, held monthly, to Sunday Evening Tea, 
held each week, is also a decided gain. This has made 
the building attractive on Sunday evenings, and is one of 
the most promising new features in the year’s work. 


Educational Opportunities. 


The Educational Department shows a slight gain in the 
number of students over last year, and the high character 


20 


of teaching work has been maintained. A visit from 
Messrs. E. L. Shuey, of Dayton, Ohio, and Geo. B. Hodge, 
of New York City, in February, when a Conference with 
our Educational Committee, and with a representative 
group of business men was arranged, proved most sugges- 
tive and stimulating. The Committee has endeavored to 
profit by this help in planning for future work. At the 
same time our Educational Department urgently needs 
enlargement. We have done a large and growing work 
for young men in commercial branches of study, but have 
not been able to meet the need of the industrial classes of 
young men to anything like the same degree. Your Direc- 
tors would present as one of the most urgent present 
needs of the Association, the space and equipment which 
would enable the Educational Committee to touch 
machine shop practice, forging, pattern making and 
related subjects for the benefit of the large number of 
young men in the city in those callings. 


The Physical Work. 

“The Young Men’s Christian Association to-day is the 
leading factor in Physical Training; it has 500 gym- 
nasiums, as against 270 in the colleges, 300 Turners’ 
organizations and 100 Athletic Clubs, thus outnumbering 
any other single organization in Physical Work. The 
Association now enrolls in its gymnasiums fully 100,000 
men. Through their influence the Association will have 
a decided effect upon the character of the race, giving to 
future generations stronger bodies, and making better 
citizens.” 

Not only has the interest and attendance in our Physical 
Department increased during the season, but there has 
been an increase in efficiency as well. The Directors 
would draw special attention to the detailed report. 


Work for Boys, 


The continued growth of the boys’ work has been one of 
the most encouraging features of the year, and the reach- 
ing out to other sections of the city by the organization 


21 


' 


of the North-East Branch, and the conduct of work for 
boys at the Railroad Branch at Point St. Charles, is full 
of promise for the future. There has been a better adap- 
tation of the religious, social and physical work for the 
boys in the Building, necessitated by the growing 
membership and by a better understanding of what the 
boys need. Most encouraging religious results have been 
seen in the regular work at the Building, as well as in the 
Summer Camp, which last year reached an attendance of 
sixty boys—the largest in its history. The Evening Edu- 
cational Classes for working boys, begun so successfully 
last year, were further extended this year and have opened 
up a new field for development. A conference with Mr. 
E, M. Robinson, of the International Committee, in April, 
was of great value to the Committee. The urgent need 
here is for such addition to our present building as would 
enable us to accommodate a boys’ membership of from 600 
to 1,000, embodying work for boys in all branches similar 
to that of the young men. 


The Religious Work. 


A strong Christian desire and purpose has pervaded the 
entire work of the Association, largely due to the influence 
and effectiveness of the weekly religious meetings and 

sible Classes. These have been regularly maintained 
with good results, comparing favorably with former years. 
Of special note this year is the formation of a successful 
sible class for gymnasium men, conducted by our Physical 
Director; the visit of Rey. Elmore Harris, D.D., of Toronto, 
during the Week of Prayer, and the series of Conferences 
on our religious work in December, January and March. 
In these latter we are indebted to Mr. C. M. Copeland, of 
Toronto, and Mr. F. 8S. Goodman, of New York City, for 
valuable counsel and assistance. Greater effort has been 
made to reach young men outside of the building, as seen 
in the faithful work of the Invitation Committee, and 
young men coming as strangers to the city have been 
sought out and welcomed to the hospitality and priviliges 
of the Association in greater numbers, perhaps, than ever 


22 

before. There has been constant endeavor to relate young 
men to the churches of the city, and 72 such have been 
introduced to the pastors during the year. At least 17 
young men began the Christian life at the instance of the 
Association, and 19 of our members that we know of 
joined the churches in this city last year, of which 13 were 
directly influenced to this step by the Association. The 
practical agencies of the Employment Bureau, Boarding 
House Register, sick visitation and relief to unfortunate 
young men, continue a most helpful ministration. The 
work at the Militia Camp was successfully conducted this 
year at Three Rivers. 


Growth. 

In reviewing the past year’s work, the Directors are 
filled with gratitude to God for the results secured, In 
every Department increase and advancement has been 
apparent. 

This work must grow as the city grows. No thoughtful 
citizen can fail to be impressed with the future of this 
city. From all sections of the world young men are 
coming to our doors. In looking forward to the future 
the Directors realize that constant calls for larger expen- 
diture will be inevitable if we are to fulfil our trust. The 
necessity for securing a larger contributing constituency 
is emphasized each year. Increased amounts should be 
sought from our present subscribers who are familiar with 
the work, and in addition the committee should endeavor 
to secure at least two hundred new contributors who 
would give from five to ten dollars annually. 


A Liberal Endowment Fund. 


is also required to enlarge the present work and open up 
new lines, and the Directors would earnestly call the 
attention of the members and citizens to the following 
needs: 


First—An Annex to this Building, 


The Association entered this Building eleven years ago. 
Many thousands of young men have passed through its 


99 
23 


membership, and been materially helped by means of the 
privileges offered. It was then felt that sufficient space 
had been provided for many years to come, but all the 
Departments have shown such a steady and permanent 
growth, that enlargement is absolutely necessary. The 
more recent buildings are being equipped with two gym- 
nasiums—one for men and one for boys. This need is 
most urgent here. It would enable the Association to 
take immediate advantage of the unparalleled opportunity 
now open for doing a more extensive physical work for the 
young men and boys of the city. 

In addition to the present Educational Class accommo- 
dation, a whole floor is needed where technical training 
may be afforded to the ever-increasing number of the 
industrial class of young men in our city. This field is 
absolutely free for the Association to enter, and would 
produce excellent results both to the young men who are 
seeking such help, and to the manufacturers of the city, 
who are always on the outlook for men with better train- 
ing and experience. 

The work for boys is perhaps the most urgent. Unusual 
progress has been made during the past year. Two 
Branches have been opened in other sections of the city, 
and the work in this Building increased. The Committee 
has rendered most loyal and efficient service. The possi- 
bilities for this field of work are very great. Prevention 
is so much better and more economical than reformation. 
In other cities separate Buildings are now being erected 
and devoted wholly to work for boys. The unwisdom as 
well as the difficulty of carrying on work for men and boys 
in the same rooms is apparent. <A great mass of boys 
leave school at twelve and fourteen years of age for busi- 
ness. Work for these must be done at night. They 
require separate Educational classes and privileges in all 
departments. The Association is the only agency in the 
field equipped to do this work. The importance is 
paramount. 

Fortunately this Association owns a lot adjoining the 
present Building, 66 x 64. Here an annex could be erected 
at comparatively small cost, which would give the gym- 


24 


asium space needed, also a floor for this Junior work, and 
another for the Educational work. It could be added to 
the present plant, so that its supervision might be econo- 
mically administered. What a splendid investment with 
such immediate returns in sight! 
We confidently hope that this opportunity may be 
accepted by some friend or friends of the boys and young 
men of our city. 


Second—Evening Educational Work. 


A large income for the extension and supervision of 
Educational class work. The need has been demonstrated 
beyond a question. 


Third—Religious Addresses and Bible Stndy Courses. 

A fund which would enable the Association to bring on 
a number of the leading men of the country each year, who 
are specially qualified to address young men, also for 
maintaining Bible Courses adapted to the needs of men. 


Fourth—For Working Boys. 

A fund to supply facilities and maintain work suited to 
the needs of boys, in different sections of the city. 
Fifth—The Association Library. 


An endowment to enable us to build up and maintain a 
distinctive Young Men’s Library, which would be a great 
blessing to future generations. 


Sixth—For an Athletic Field, if Possible with Water Front. 


A fund which would secure and maintain such a field, 
where members could have the opportunity of outdoor 
recreation and athletic sport. 


The. Staff. 


The following changes were made on the staff during 
the year. Mr. W. H. Ball, the Association’s first Physical 
Director, who rendered such helpful service during the 


past ten years in directing the Physical training and 
development of the members, resigned and accepted a simi- 
lar position with the Prospect Park Branch of the Brooklyn 
Association. He was succeeded by Mr. J. E. Merritt, 
from the same Branch of the Brooklyn Association, who 
has continued on the work most acceptably, and won the 
esteem and confidence of the members. 

Mr. F. EK. Burgess, who has rendered most pains-taking 
and self-sacrificing service in the Educational Department 
for the past three years, resigned on May 1st to enter 
business. 

Mr. John Roy, who has had charge of the Membership, 
Social and Employment work, expects to leave on Sept. Ist, 
to enter the Association Training School, Springfield, 
Mass., and also Mr. A. B. Dawson, the Assistant Physical 
Director, leaves in September, to enter the same school for 
«a further course in physical work. These men will have 
the best wishes of all our members, for their future 
success in the work. 


In Memoriam. 


Death has been very busy during the year, and we have 
{uo record the loss of a large number of our subscribers and 
members.

MEMBERSHIP. 


The Membership Committee have closed another year of 
work, and are grateful for the results accomplished, These 
have been due to faithful work on the part of members of 
the Committee. 

Last year the Association received the largest revenue 
from members and also had the largest membership in its 
history, and we are pleased to record that there has been 
a further increase in both members and revenue in the 
year just closed. The statement is as follows:— 


Total receipts from membership:—

Estimated receipts for the year at the opening were.. ..$8,000.00

There are a number of gentlemen supporting the Asso- 
ciation at present with a subscription yearly of $5.00 and 
$10.00, who might be induced to give a larger sum for a 
definite purpose. In this connection it might be a matter 
for consideration whether a “ Membership Endowment 
Fund” might not be instituted. To this any one who 
would contribute, say $200, would have the knowledge that 
the Association would put this sum aside and use the 
interest for money invested toward giving a membership 


ot 


to any one deserving such and not having it within their 
means to pay for it. The party making such donation 
would, if they wished, intimate any one to take advantage 
of its benefits, and if they did not so nominate any one, 
the Association would do so and advise them of it, thus 
giving them a personal interest in the work and in some 
young man. 

During the year the Membership Committee, in con- 
junction with the Social Committee, through the king 
assistance of friends, purchased two tables of Ping- 
pong. These have been constantly used, and have 
been the means of drawing a number of members together, 
and also others to the Building. The more the member- 
ship can be brought together and made to feel an active 
interest in the work of the Association and in each other, 
so much the better, and the Committee feel that to accom- 
plish this any legitimate means should be used. Games 
in which all may be more or less interested are a splendid 
means to this end. 

The results of the past year have been attained chiefly 
by holding as far as lay in the Committee’s power, the 
interest of old members, while, of course, new memvers 
were secured also. The Committee for the ensuing year 
will have the task of mainly looking for new sources from 
which to recruit the membership of the Association. 


CHARLES T. HARE, 
‘ Chairman. 


REPORTS OF COMMITTEES. 


RELIGIOUS DEPARTMENT. 


The religious work of the Association is not by any 
means confined to the stated meetings and Bible classes, 
yet these afford special opportunity for the development 
and expression of the religious life. 

The following reports of the sub-committees will give 
fuller details :— 


Saturday Night Meeting. 


Your Committee are grateful for the past year’s work 
and encouraged for the future. The average attendance 
for the year was 62, an increase of 12 over the previous 
year. We feel that this is due largely to the faithful 
efforts of the Invitation Committee, who have been on 
hand every night. There is still room for improvement in 
the attendance, however, and the Committee would like to 
recommend the meeting to many of our Christian young 
men as an opportunity for work in helping other men. We 
are assured that the meetings during the year were helpful 
to not a few men. inquirers were dealt with fre- 


to non-Christians to begin the Christian life. 


JAS. R. GREIG. 


Sunday Morning Bible Class. 


This class has continued regularly throughout the 
year studying the International Sunday-School lessons. 
39 different men have been members of the class, with a 
total attendance of 491, and an average of ten. 


J. K. McNUTT. 


36 
Sunday Afternoon Bible Class. 


The total attendance for the year was 3,092, an average 
of 60 per Sunday. This is a slight falling off compared 
with the previous year, but an increase over two years 
ago. Early in the year we finished “The Study of the 
Lives of Prominent Men of the Bible,” and since then we 
have followed an outlined study in the Gospel of John 
with topical studies. This course has been of great help 
to the class members, and is being followed up with deep 
interest. At each meeting note has been taken of stran- 
gers who have attended, and they were written to during 
the following week, and invited to become regular 
members of the class. Letters were also sent out from 
time to time to absent members, besides personal calls 
being made. A number of our members have gone from 
the class into Sunday School work during the year, and 
op Dec. 22nd, instead of our regular service a Christmas 
service of song was held. Kind friends assisted in the 
service, and a delightful hour was spent. On Easter 
Sunday a special service was held, at which Mr. Budge 
gave an address on the meaning of “ The Resurrection.” 
The following friends kindly assisted with the music:— 
Mrs. Kingman, Mr. Hubert A. Baker, and Mr. D. W. 
Wilson. Attendance, 110. The class gave a donation of 
$10.00 toward the current expenses of the Association, and 
the Treasurer reports all accounts. paid with a small 
balance on hand. The class greatly appreciates the faith- 
ful services of Mr. W. T. Walmsley as organist, and Mr. 
Harry Griffiths, leader of the singing. 

The thanks of the Committee and class are due ‘to the 
Ladies’ Committee, for flowers for our table each Sunday, 
and to the following gentlemen who conducted the class in 
the absence of Mr. Budge: Rev. Mr. Tinling, Mr. W. M. 
Oatts, of Glasgow; Mr. Jas. McConaughy, Mount Hermon; 
Mr. W. H. Ball, and Mr. C. K. Calhoun. 

We earnestly ask the prayers and support of a larger 
number of men, that a greater blessing may come upon the 


class during the next year. 
J.J. SLOAN. 


ae) 
~~ 


Invitation Committee. 


This Committee reports a most successful season. — It 
was re-organized at the beginning of September, with a 
membership of 15, and during the year has had an average 
of eight men on duty each Saturday evening. From Sept. 
28th to date, upwards of 35,000 invitations have been 
distributed on the streets, and in various places where 
men publicly resort. We believe the work of the 
committee has had a most decided effect in increasing the 
attendance of both the Saturday evening and Sunday 
afternoon meetings, and there is encouraging evidence 
that many men have been thereby influenced for Christ. 

Your Committee would suggest that this work might be 
considerably enlarged so as to bring the Association more 
prominently before the public. Means should be devised 
for better advertising in public places so as to attract the 
attention of the large numbers of people who frequent 
public places. 

H. T. SOMERS. 


Hospital Service. , 

The Sunday morning service at the Western Hospital 
has been conducted during the year by the Committee in 
charge, and has been thoroughly appreciated by the 
patients, and the words of thanks which they have express- 
ed have been many. Throughout the year we have been 
assisted in the musical part of the service by several young 
ladies from Erskine Church Y. P. 8. ©. E., and Emmanuel 
Church, as well as others to whom our thanks are due. 


THOS. M. BARRINGTON. 


Sunday Afternoon Men’s Meeting. 


Encouraged by the success of last year, the Men’s 
Meeting has been held regularly from Oct. 6th,, and is 
being continued throughout the month of May. In all 
twenty-eight meetings have been held, with a total atten- 
dance of 2,719, and an average of 97. Good interest has 


38 


been shown throughout the season, and more definite 
results have been apparent than last year. Whenever 
suitable opportunity offered the question of personal 
decision for the Christian life has been urged, and on 
several occasions there have been requests for prayer, and 
enquirers dealt with. We have been favored with addresses 
from outside speakers as follows:—Rey. R. P. Kerr, D.D., 
Richmond, Virginia; Rev. Elmore Harris, D.D., Toronto; 
James McConaughy, Mount Hermon; Fred. 8. ‘Goodman, 
New York City. On March 23rd and 380th, the meeting 
was merged into the meetings for men held in St. James 
Methodist Church, conducted by Ev angelists Turk and 
Kerby, and our Committee lent their co-operation. Our 
thanks are due to the local pastors, who have cheerfully 
co-operated by speaking at the meetings, and those who 
have so kindly and efficiently assisted with the musical 
services. In September we took advantage of the presence 
of Rey. John MeNeill in the city over Sunday, and a mass 
meeting for men was arranged in the American Presbyter- 
ian Church, when about one thousand men were present 


Bible Study. 


Commencing, Tuesday, October 29th, two Bible Training 
Classes were conducted each Tuesday evening at seven 
o’clock, until the end of April. The one class under Mr. 
Budge followed a course of studies in “Paith and Con- 
duct,” with an average attendance of 12, and the other, 
under Mr. Calhoun, “The History of the Apostolic Church,” 
average atendance, 14. These classes have done much to 
give the men closer views of the Bible, and led to greater 
development in the Christian life. 

In connection with the Week of Prayer, Nov. 9-17, 1901, 
the Association arranged for a visit from Rev. Elmore 
Harris, D.D., of Toronto. Dr. Harris addressed the Satur- 
day and Sunday meetings at the beginning and close of the 
week, and conducted afternoon and evening meetings in 
the Associatiom Building during the week. These were 
greatly enjoyed by all, and greatly stimulated the Chris- 
tian activity of the Association. The meetings were 


3f 
practical also in leading a number to begin the Christian 
life. The Association is deeply indebted to Dr. Harris for 
the splendid service thus rendered and will always 
welcome a similar visit. 

The usual Christmas morning service was conducted by 
Mr. Budge, with good attendance and interest. 

A series of three special Conferences on our religious 
work were held on Dec. 12th, Jan. 16th, and March 14th 
and 15th, attended by the members of all our Committees 
and representatives from the other Departments. At the 
first of these Conferences Mr. ©. M. Copeland, Provincial 
Secretary, was present, and spoke. He also rendered 
valuable counsel. The second conference followed up a 
programme previously outlined and discussed it in detail. 
At the third Mr. Fred. S. Goodman, Secretary of the Inter- 
national Committee, conducted two evening meetings, 
which were attended by the majority of our entire 
Committee force, at which a progressive policy for the 
future was outlined and adopted. 

We were favored with a visit from Mr. John R. Mott, 
Senior College Secretary of the International Committee, 
on March 21st, when he spoke at a public meeting in the 
American Presbyterian Church, reviewing his recent trip 
in the Orient, and recounting the remarkable experiences 
which accompanied his visit there. There was a large 
attendance and great interest developed in the foreign 
work of the Association. 

As in former years, the friends kindly granted permis- 
sion to the Association to erect a tent for Association 
purposes, at the Militia Camp in Three Rivers, June 28th 
to July 6th. Work was carried on amongst the men 
during the camp with good results, under the supervision 
of Mr. John Roy. Words of appreciation from both 
officers and men show that this practical work by the 
Association meets a work needed. 

While it is difficult to state results accurately, the fol- 
lowing figures will indicate somewhat:—72 young men 
were introduced to pastors, most of them directly with 
reference to church membership. 17 young men began 


40 


the Christian life through the Association, and 19 of our 
members that we know of, joined churches in the city 
during the year, of whom 13 were definitely influenced to 
this step through the Association. 


EMPLOYMENT BUREAU. 


During the past year this Department has come in touch 
with 430 men and boys, who have filled applications and 
given us an opportunity to be of service to them. Through 
several sources 318 vacancies were heard of, and we have 
been able to secure 76 permanent and a number of tempor- 
ary position for those applying. The greater number of 
these men were strangers, not only to the Association, but 
to the city; many have been invited to the Strangers’ Tea 
and religious meetings, and through these have become 
interested in the Association, so that a number have 
become members, and are now using the privileges. 


SOCIAL DEPARTMENT. 


The Committee has pleasure in presenting this report of 
Social work, carried on during the year, which includes 
entertainment of members, by means of Parlor Games, 
“At Homes,” and Concerts. 

The principal event of the year was the New Year's 
Reception, which, as formerly, was a decided success in 
point of attendance and in the evident appreciation of our 
guests. Criticisms have been noted, thoroughly discussed 
in Committee, and will be remembered when planning for 
the next Annual event. 

Six Socials, or “At Homes,” were given to members and 
their friends, and the Committee has endeavored, and we 
hope, succeeded, in sending an invitation to every member 
of the Association for one of these gatherings. Parlor 
games were purchased, and the programme each evening 
consisted of games, music and refreshments. The members 


5 


41 


have appreciated these evenings and we hope that acquain- 
tanceship has been extended and valued friendships 
formed. 

Two tables and sets of the popular game, Ping-Pong, 
have been placed in the Building by the members of the 
Membership and Social Committees. The tables have 
been, and are still, in continual use, and we feel satisfied 
that they add greatly to the social enjoyment of the 
members. 

In the month of November a Social Department Confer- 
ence was held. Former members of the Social, Reception 
and Strangers’ Tea Committees were invited to attend, 
and the social work was thoroughly discussed. Many 
yaluable suggestions were made, but were too late to be 
acted upon without interfering with plans already made. 
They should be well considered by the committee in prepar- 
ing the programme for next year. 

We take this opportunity of expressing our appreciation 
of the services so willingly rendered by the Ladies’ Com- 
mittee, and must confess that if any success has attended 
the work of this Department it has been due in a large 
measure, to their kindly assistance. 

This report would be incomplete did we not express our 
deep appreciation of the work of the Association Orchestra 
during the year, under the leadership of Mr. Chas. Reich- 
ling. The weekly rehersals took place as usual, and 
special assistance was rendered at the New Year’s and 
other Receptions. 

The Committee reported having held seven monthly Teas 
to which were invited strangers and members who had 
recently joined the Association, a number of 408. The 
attendance quite equalled former years. About the 
middle of February it was felt advisable to change these 
monthly Teas to weekly, allowing any member of the 
Association to attend on payment of a small fee, in addi- 
tion to strangers, who were invited guests. Since Feb. 
23rd, ten of these Teas have been held, with an 
average attendance of 25, and have proved a grand success. 
They have been under the direction of representatives from 


42 


the Religious, Social, Educational and Physical Depart- 
ment Committees in turn. 
ALEC ARTHUR. 


Reception Committee. 


The Committee begs to report that as far as possible it 
has provided men for the reception floor during the 
evenings of the past year, and has received and shown 
around our building over two hundred and fifty visitors 
from all parts of the world. 

The members of the Committee have assisted the Social 
Committee at the monthly socials. They also assisted in 
sending a delegate to the Berlin convention. 

Since May 1st, 1901, twenty-one different members have 
served on the Committee but for the above named reasons 
ten of these have had to resign. 

We hope during the summer to keep the Committee in 
full strength, and are preparing a neat card giving infor- 
mation about our work, which will be distributed to visi- 
tors whom we shall meet. 

JAS. K. McNUTT, 


EDUCATIONAL DEPARTMENT. 


The Committee arranged this year for courses of study 
in twelve branches, covering twenty-five weeks, from 
October Ist, to April lst. Three hundred and fifty-nine 
different students enrolled in thirty-five weekly classes. 
The enrollment is a gain of twelve over the previous year. 
The total enrollment was five hundred and forty-five. 

A general course in English literature of the Victorian 
period was substituted for the class in Shakespeare of last 
year. <A class in Mathematics was added this year as an 
experiment, also a class in Physics, both of which have 
proved to be a move in the right direction. ‘The course in 
“ Municipal Government and its Betterment,” by Alderman 
H. B. Ames, attracted a large number of newly enfranchis- 


45 


ed young men, and proved most interesting. 53 students 
wrote on the International Examinations at the end of the 
season. Forty-two of these were passed by our local 
Examiners, and their papers forwarded to the Internation- 
al Board for final examination. 

The Glee Club was under the leadership of Mr. Horace 
W. Reyner, Mus. Bac., with a membership of twenty, and a 
successful season’s work culminated with a concert in 
Association Hall. 

The Banjo, Mandolin and Guitar Club was organized this 
year for the first time with a membership of eighteen. Mr. 
J. J. Lavert was the leader. For a first year organization 
a fair measure of success was achieved. 

The statement of class attendance is as follows:—

Social intercourse amongst the students was promoted 
by the several classes meeting for tea during the season. 


44 


The interest in the studies tends to increase as the men 
become better acquainted. 

The Second Annual Supper of the Department was held 
on Thursday evening, April 10th, when about eighty 
students were present. Among the responses to the Toast 
List were addresses of special note by Messrs. Abner King- 
man and H. B. Ames. 

A. M. MACKAY. 


READING ROOM AND LIBRARY, 


The Committee have endeavored to maintain and to 
increase the efficiency of the Reading Room, and have 
placed on file 152 periodicals, a larger number than that of 
any previous year. These have cost $276.45, of which sum 
$84.00 was raised by the annual sale of papers and maga- 
zines in December. The following additions have been 
made for the current year:—The Sphere, London Musical 
Times, The Musician, Peargon’s Magazine, The American 
Debater, Physical Training, The Association Seminar, 
Gunton’s Magazine, World Wide, Mind and Body, Forest 
and Stream, Amateur Work, The World’s Work, Every- 
body’s Magazine, and the Inland Printer. The bill of fare 
thus presented will, we believe, provide wholesome food 
for every taste, however varied. 

During the past summer the much-needed work of re- 
-ataloguing the Library was undertaken and completed. 
The room also has been greatly improved by the addition 
of a book counter, with shelves beneath. Owing to these 
improvements, the Library was closed for nearly three 
months, and the total issue of books, therefore, shows a 
diminution, being 6,581, as compared with 7,665 for last 
year. 

A comparison by months during which the Library was 
open, however, shows in every instance, an advance for the 
current year. 

291 new books have been added during the year, the 
greater number of which have been placed in the Depart- 


45 


“ment of History, Science and General Literature. The 
number of issues from these sections has been consider- 
ably increased, and the preponderance of Fiction has been 
decreased by two percent, as compared with last year. 

The Referencee Library has been strengthened by 
several valuable additions, as The Expositor’s Bible, 
Whryte’s Bible Characters, Supplement to the Encyclo- 
paedia Britannica, Literature of all Nations. 

The Committee desire to record their hearty apprecia- 
tion of the faithful services of Mr. Burgess, the librarian 
for the past three years. It is, in their opinion, mainly 
owing to his labours and watchful care that the Library 
and Reading Room are in better condition than ever 
before. 

I. GAMMELL. 


PHYSICAL DEPARTMENT. 


In presenting the report of the Physical Department we 
are glad to report a prosperous year, in both attendance 
and interest. There has also been created an exception- 
ally fine feeling of fellowship among our members. ‘The 
committee feel that this is due, in a large measure, to the 
influence of the Gymnasium Men’s Bible Study Club—our 
youngest organization. All the Clubs have had a success- 
ful year, as will be noted later in their respective reports. 

At the beginning of the season’s work Dr. W.S. Morrow 
was obliged to resign as medical examiner. Dr. F. W. 
Gilday has been with us during the entire year, and the 
thanks of the Committee are due him for the efficient 
service he rendered. 

At the beginning of the season it was found necessary 
to divide the elementary class and schoolboys’ class into 
two sections, in order to handle the number. This division 
to a large degree accounts for the increased average atten- 
dance, because it provided room for all, and more attention 
could be given to the individual, thereby adding materially 
to the quality of the work. 


46 


This season a change was made in the gymnasium 
closing, and in place of the usual exhibition, the Committee 
felt that a Banquet would be of greater help to the Asso- 
ciation. Its great success proved the wisdom of the 
change. 


Leaders’ Corps. 


The Corps, through its members, has rendered valuable 
and willing assistance to our Physical Director on the 
gymnasium floor, in the examining room, in exhibition 
work and also in the Bible Study Club. <A very helpful 
course of lectures was delivered by our Physical Director 
during the season. The Seventh Annual Banquet was 
held on March 6th, and was a great success. One of the 
finest affairs during the season was the first Annual 
Banquet of the Department, conducted by the Corps. 
There were 175 present. The Corps enrolls in its active 
membership 22 men. 

The thanks of the Committee are due this Corps for the 
services so efficiently rendered to the Physical Director and 
his Assistant. 


Things to Aim for Next Year. 


1. Increased accommodation for boys and intermediate 
departments in a larger gymnasium. 

2. Securing of athletic grounds. 

3. A more extended policy in presenting opportunities 
of physical exercise in the gymnasium to business men. 

4, A more complete system of securing names of young 
men not attending the Association and presenting the 
work and opportunities of the Association through the 
Physical Department. 

In conclusion we desire to say that the success of this 
department of the work in all its branches is in no small 
measure due to the faithful work of Mr. Merritt, who has 
constantly kept a threefold aim before him, endeavoring 
to perfect the spiritual, mental and physical life of the 
members. The same spirit seems to have manifested 
itself with all members of the Physical Committee. 


Ay

The Elementary, Business Men’s, Junior and Boys’ 
classes show a large increase over last year. 

The total number of members registered in the classes 
is 631, an increase of 59 over last year. New members 
examined; young men, 296; boys, 147. Total, 448. There 
were also many members re-examined during the year. 


Gymnasium Men’s Bible Study Club. 


This Club was organized on Noy. 3rd, 1901, and seemed 
to fill a long-felt want in this Department. The Club met 
every Sunday for twenty-six weeks, at 5.15, for three-quar- 
ters of an hour, and at six o’clock had tea together, each 
member paying his share. The subject for the year was, 
“ Life Questions and Answers.” The class has undoubted- 
ly had a great effect upon the work in the gymnasium. Men 
from all the classes have attended. It has been a power in 
assimilating and binding together the men of the various 
classes, and these men have in turn given a higher tone to 
all the work in the gymnasium. Three of our members 
are enlisted in the service of the Empire in South Africa. 
We trust they may be spared to return to us. A photo- 
graph of the class taken in March was presented to the 
Association at the Annual Banquet. This picture well 
represented the different classes the Club touched. There 
were in the group 11 leaders, 15 elementary men, 8 inter- 
mediate, 4 advanced, and 7 no class. The total attendance 
for 26 sessions was 844, an ayerage of 32. 


45 


Your Committee desires to take this opportunity of 
placing on record the pleasure it has given them to co-ope- 
nate with Mr. Merritt, our leader, and we feel sure that 
next season the class will be of greater service both to the 


men and to the Department. 
GEORGE E. WINTER. 


Bicycle Club. 


The Club had one of the most sociable years of its nine 
years existence. In addition to the ordinary events there 
were excursions, receptions, ladies’ rides, trolley rides, 
surprise parties, etc. These being the only social features 
in the Association during the summer season, it is needless 
to say that they were well attended and enjoyed by all. 

The Treasurer’s statement shows a cash balance of $2.07. 


A. E. SMAILL. 


Tennis Clnb. 

Fresh air and wholesome exercise is a necessity for 
everyone. Whether through knowledge of this principle 
or otherwise, many of our members have availed them- 
selves of the opportunity afforded by our Club to secure 
fresh air, exercise and pleasure combined. Membership 
numbers 48 in all. 

Four courts were equipped and utilized to their full 
extent every evening, weather permitting. Grounds 
adjoin the Western Hospital. 

In regard to competition with outside Clubs, as usual, 
we joined the City Intermediate League, and losing our 
first match with St. Lamberts, were declared out of the list 
in accordance with the manner in which the schedule was 
drawn up, which was unsatisfactory to us 

The financial statement shows a balance of $10.86. 


F. W. SHARP. 
Cricket Club. 


In the month of May, 1901, there was convened in the 
Association Parlors, a small but enthusiastic gathering of 


49 


young men, the majority hailing from the mother-land 
across the seas. When the meeting came to a close the 
Y. M. C. A. Cricket Club was an accomplished fact. The 
numbers were steadily added to and a very successful 
season passed, during which the Club played nine matches, 
winning five. The Treasurer’s report shows a balance of 
$1.34 to the good. 
N. L. MARTIN. 


Hockey Club. 


Permission was obtained from the Directors’ Committee 
to enter the Junior Hockey League which was successfully 
effected. It will probably be thought at first sight that 
the team had no success; but we think, considering the 
close score, in every instance but one, and the experience 
of the teams with which we competed, that for a new 
ageregation, we made a fairly good showing. The poor 
ice accommodation, and the class of teams played, were a 
great drawback. 

Our membership numbered 37. Credit balance on hand 
$1.82. 

J. M. ANDERSON. 


Bowling Alleys. 


The Bowling season began in December, and has continu- 
ed up to the present time. There seems to be an increasing 
number anxious to use the alleys as the time goes on, so 
that at the end of the season we have many more bowlers 
than at the beginning. A number are attracted by the 
competitions, and so learn to bowl that they may have a 
part in them. During the season two of these Competi- 
tions have been held. First one for individuals, in which 
four prizes were offered and thirteen men contested, and 
then a team competition, four teams taking part, in this 
the winning team received a prize and also two individual 
prizes were given. The Club closes its year with a credit 
balance of $22.28. 

F. SLOCOMBE. 


or 
oO 


Basebali Club. 


We are happy to report that last season was the most 
successful in the history of the Club. During the season 
eight exhibition games were played and five League games. 
The club was victorious in every League game, thereby 
winning the amateur championship of the city. Member- 
ship numbered 39. The report of the Treasurer shows 
that the Club came out just even. The suits of last season 
were a great addition to the appearance of the team. 


A. G. BURTON. 
Athletic Club. 


The Montreal baseball grounds were secured for the 
season, for three evenings each week. 

During the summer months a series of weekly Handicaps 
were run off with some success, and proved of great inter- 
est to the members. We think that this might be improved 
upon by having them arranged earlier in the sason, and 
would recommend that prizes be given. ; 

The attendance at the grounds varied from ten to 
twenty-five, which showed a decided increase over the 
previous year. 

The Annual Field Day was held in September, and 
proved the most successful one ever held, the different 
events being keenly contested. There were 69 individuals 
entered and two Association records broken. The atten- 
dance was unusually large. 

The season was brought to a close with a very enjoyable 
sleigh drive, over ninety being present. 

The statement of the Treasurer shows a credit balance 
of $2.03. 

F. W. HADWIN. 


Snowshoe Club. 


The Snowshoe Club has had a most successful season. 
The securing of new blanket suits for the Club was a great 
factor in the good appearance of the Club in all of its turn 
cuts. Both the members’ and the ladies’ tramps were well 


51 


attended. The annual “ At Home” of the Club was held 
at the close of the season, with an attendance of over one 
hundred. The financial statement shows an eyen balance. 


*SEORGE E. WINTER. 


JUNIOR DEPARTMENT REPORT FOR 1901-02. 


In looking back over the past season’s work your Com- 
mittee are impressed with the progress that has been made 
in almost every branch of the Department. 

The present Membership is: 


CHO OUMS OMA inuan cs —eilies tt eet cot ees, POUL 
IDUSINOSSUDOVS).. 6 4 4 <5 Se ea wo Ae 
Malang a) tote] Ofetwnts At eer hea bese 


an increase of 50 over the previous year. 

The work for boys has not been strictly confined to the 
members of the Department, but has reached out to other 
sections of the City, and, including the Branch Work, more 
than 400 boys have come under Association influences; and 
during the past two months the combined religious 
meetings have averaged 117. 

Thirty boys graduated into the Senior Department 
during the year. 


Religious. 


The Friday Night Meeting has been conducted regularly 
throughout the past year for Boys from 14 to 16 years of 
age, and this year a similar meeting every Friday after- 
noon for those from 12 to 14. Not only has a greater 
number of boys been reached through this age division, but 
it is also felt that larger and better results have been 
attained. 

The Christian boys in the Department number 80, thirty 
of whom have been attending the Bible Training Classes. 


52 


Week by week four Bible Training Classes, under the 
leadership of Messrs. A. L. Paterson, H. G. Beall, John 
Brown and L. Cushing, have been regularly and faithfully 
attended by the boys. One class, finding it difficult to 
come to the Association Building, has met in the various 
homes of its members, in Westmount. 

As a result of the Religious Work, nine boys have been 
directly led to unite with their Churches. 

A prominent part of our Sunday work is the monthly 
Song Service at the General Hospital, and the patients 
having given many expressions of appreciation, the 
number of services has been doubled. Much of the success 
has been due to the leadership of Mr. Montignani. 

The following figures show the average attendance at 
the Religious Meetings for the past two years:— 


1901-2. 1900-1. 
Friday Night Meeting ..... 32 34 
Friday Afternoon Meeting .. 21 


—53 
Bible Training Classes (4)... 22 6 


Hospital Serviee-. 32. 2. 26 14 


Educational. 


Classes in Bookkeeping, Penmanship, Arithmetic and 
Shorthand have been successfully conducted for the Busi- 
ness Boys. Out of a total enrollment of 51 different 
pupils, there was an average attendance of 30, being about 
60 per cent. Samples of work in each class were secured 
at the end of the Courses. 

On December 19 and January 30 two very practical 
business talks were given by Mr. A. Kingman and Mr. 
D. W. Ross, respectively. 

The Library has been made use of by 224 Members, 
which, considering the small amount available for new 
books, is certainly remarkable. 

The Reading and, Recreation Rooms have been well 
patronized. 


53 
Social. 

Limited space absolutely prohibits our giving a compre- 
hensive report on the Social Work. Never in the history 
of the Department has such an enjoyable Winter been 
passed, and the Young Ladies’ Committee appointed last 
Fall, has contributed largely to the success of this work. 

Apart from the Opening and Closing Entertainments 
the plan of small group Socials was carried out with splen- 
did results. 

Three Receptions were held for New Members during the 
first part of the Season. Socials were also held for the 
Junior School Boys, Senior School Boys, and Business 
Boys. 

Mention might also be made of the Annual Sleigh Drive 
and Camp Reunion. 

The Opening Entertainment for Boys only, had an 
attendance of 350, and was the means of bringing in quite 
a number of New Members. 

Instead of combining the Closing Exhibition and Concert 
on the same evening, as heretofore, these this year have 
been held on different evenings, the Exhibition coming off 
on the 17th April, and the Closing Entertainment on the 
29th, at which there were present upwards of 500, includ- 
ing a large number of parents and friends. 

Six All Day Outings were held during the summer, with 
an average attendance of 18. These were effective in 
keeping the fellows together during the summer months. 

The Business Boys have lately formed a Club under the 
title of “The Mutual Improvement Club,” which already 
has a membership of 37. 


Physical. 


The division of the School Boys’ Gymnasium Classes 
into two sections (12 to 14, and 14 to 16 years of age) has 
been a distinct improvement, as is seen by the increased 
attendance, which has averaged as follows:— 


o4+ 


1901-2. 1900-1. 
Senior School Boys’ Class... 15 


Junior : ee as BE 
—52 47 
Business Boys’ Class....... 41 34 


Basketball Tournaments have been conducted in both 
the School and Business Boys’ Classes and Photos taken 
of the winning Teams. 


Junior Camp. 


Owing to the differences in the ages and inclinations of 
the boys, the Camp was divided into two sections, viz: 


Business Boys .... . .June 15-29. 
School ... . dune 29-July 13. 


The success of both Camps amply justified the wisdom 
of this step. 

The Business Boys’ Camp, with an attendance of 17, was 
in charge of Mr. C. 8. Paterson, assisted by Dr. J. R. Cox 
and Mr. J. P. Severs. 

The School Boys’ Camp, under Mr. John Brown, was 
from every standpoint considered to be the best one ever 
held, good weather prevailing throughout the entire time. 

There were in all 43 boys, and, as usual, they enjoyed to 
the full all the pleasures of Camp life, such as fishing, 
picnics, expeditions, baseball, quoiting, athletics, swim- 
ming, ete. 

The Religious Work of the Camp is specially worthy of 
notice from the marked effect which it had upon the spirit 
of many of the boys who were there. A voluntary Bible 
Class was conducted each morning by Mr. Brown, from 
9.30 to 10, which had an average attendance of 25. 

The regular Boys Meeting held on the two Friday 
evenings was accompanied by a great spiritual blessing, 
12 boys expressing sthe desire to start the Christian life. 
This, with the short Service of Bible Reading and Prayer 
held each night in the six different Tents, did much to 


5 


oO 


maintain the spirit of manly and practical Christianity 
that pervaded everything, helping each boy to a higher and 
truer life. 

The result was in no small measure due, to the unselfish- 
ness of the efficient staff of Leaders, viz.: Messrs. A. L. 
-aterson, Alec. Peden, jr.. W. C. Montignani, D. M. 
McGavin, R. H. Macdonald and L. Cushing. 


Branch Work, 


A work for Boys has been conducted in the North-East 
section of the City, under a Committee composed of Messrs. 
W. E. Cushing, R. L. Charlton, F. A. Crowe and C. 8. Pater- 
son. 

Two Rooms were rented at 98 Mitcheson Street and 
suitably furnished; games, magazines, and a small Library 
being subsequently added. 

A Religious Meeting was held every Friday evening, and 
the Committee have reason to believe that as a result a 
number of boys have been led to accept Christ as their 
Saviour. 

The number of Boys who used the privileges of the 
Rooms were 36, and the attendance at the meetings 
averaged 16. 

Apart from the regular Meetings six Social Evenings 
were held, with an average attendance of 30. 

The cost of carrying on this work has been entirely met 
by subscriptions and donations from friends, and the 
thanks of the Committee are due to all those who so kindly 
contributed. 

A similar work has been conducted at Point St. Charles, 
in the Railroad Branch Building, under the supervision of 
Mr. Montignani, assisted by a Committee composed of 
Messrs. R. B. Ross, jr.. H. G. Beall, E. C. Budge, and 
D. A. A. MeGavin. 

The average attendance at the Meetings was 53, and we 
feel that the lives of a number of the boys have been 
touched by this work; and in the event of a Junior Depart- 
ment being formed in connection with the Railroad Branch 
a nucleus has been already secured. 


56 


To summarize the year’s work briefly we note the follow- 
ing gains :— 

50 more Members. 

117 new boys through 2 branches. 

Friday Religious Meetings, an increased attendance of 
55 per cent. 

Training Classes, an increase of 266 per cent. 

Hospital Service, an increase of 85 per cent. 

Educational Classes, an increase of 12 per cent. 

Gymnasium Classes: School Boys, an increase of 10 per 
cent.; Business Boys, an increase of 21 per cent. 

Camp, an increase of 15 per cent. 

A more effective Religious Work. 

More Faithful Bible Study. 

Better Social Work. 

Unsurpassed Camp. 

Two new Branch Departments. 

Brighter Prospects for 1902-03. 

LEMUEL CUSHING, 


THE LADIES’ COMMITTEE 


report a pleasant year’s work in all branches. 

In the Social Department, we have served at the New 
Year’s reception, and the Annual Committeemen’s Tea. In 
June, it was our privilege to share in the celebration of the 
Jubilee by serving the tea to visiting delegates and friends 
on the Monday evening. We have assisted the Social 
Committee at the Members’ Socials, which have been held 
during the winter. 

At the Opening and Closing functions of the Educa- 
tional and Physical Departments, we have had charge of 
the refreshments, and have also had a small share in the 
Sunday night Strangers’ Teas. This work in the Junior 
Department has been done by a Committee of young ladies, 
organized in December, who have rendered all possible 
assistance in the sdcial work for the boys. This Commit- 
tee has been of great help to our Committee by serving on 
several occasions during the year. 


57 


The Flower Committee has continued to supply the 
reception hall with flowers, and to send them to members 
of the Association who have been ill. These calls, we are 
glad to say, have been few, and we trust that the small 
number is not due to the fact that any have been omitted. 

A new carpet and portieres for the parlors have been 
given, and the kitchen supplied with necessary articles. 

In November, we followed the plan of last year, and held 
an open meeting for our subscribers. Our thanks are due 
to Mr. C. M. Copeland, for giving us a brief address on 
Association work. 

In order to increase the interest of the lady friends of 
the Association and to give others a share in the work 
which we enjoy so much, it has been decided to form an 
Auxiliary. 

This will be done next week, and, with larger means, we 
hope for greater usefulness in the work of this Association. 

As we disband, the Committee would take this opportun- 
ity of thanking the friends of the Association for their 
kindness and help to us during our four years’ work. 

The financial statement is as follows :—

MABEL B. WILLIAMS. 


58 
SUMMER CAMP, ST. AGATHE. 


The Permanent Camp Committee has to report the 
most successful year since its opening. 147 senior and 60 
junior members spent their vacation at this delightful 
spot, and all seemed to enjoy themselves fully. The 
committee enlarged the kitchen and built a new ice-house. 
These improvements will greatly facilitate the work. 
The Junior Committee received $617.26, and expended 
$478.67, handing over a balance of $138.59 to the Perma- 
nent Camp Committee. The Senior Camp received 
$1,306.85, and expended $1,106.96, leaving a balance of 
$199.89, which was handed to the Permanent Camp Com- 
mittee. There was expended on needed improvements 
and permanent equipment $490.89. The Camp Committee 
has reecived a loan from the Association of $384.27. This 
should be repaid next year. 

On Noy. 26th, 1901, three islands in Lac St. Joseph were 
sold by public auction ,and the Committee purchased a 
small one adjoining our present island, for $50. 


RAILROAD DEPARTMENT. 


Last year in presenting our report it was stated that 
we hoped ere long our new Building would be an establish- 
ed fact, and it is with regret that, owing to circumstances 
over which we have had no control, we are still in our old 
quarters. During the year no less than eight railroad 
men have confessed their willingness to accept the Lord 
Jesus Christ as their personal Saviour. Nineteen boys 
have also taken a stand for the Master. Our earnest 
prayer to God is that He will abundantly bless the efforts 
that shall be put forth in the year to come for the winning 
of the Railroad men to Jesus Christ. 

Railroad men 71, others 11, total 82. This shows a 
considerable falling off, numbers refusing to renew their 
membership until decision is made with reference to the 
new building. 


59 

Total, 17,750, average daily attendance, 48. 

Our Sunday afternoon meetings, held at 4.15, for Rail- 
road men, their wives and families, are proving to be one 
of the most interesting meetings held at Point St. Charles. 
Every Sunday during the year our rooms are taxed to their 
utmost capacity. 5,800 persons attended these meetings; 
average per Sunday, 111. 

On January 2nd, a boys’ work was inaugurated in con- 
nection with our Association, and has proved to be one of, 
our most successful undertakings. . Our average attendance 
is now 43. The boys meet on Thursday nights from 7 to 9; 
half an hour for games, etc., half an hour calisthenics, and 
half an hour to military drill. The remaining half hour 
being devoted to a meeting of an evangelistic nature. 
Already a marked difference is noticeable among the boys. 

Number of visits to sick and injured, 968. Emergency 
hospital used 30 times. We regret to state that we have 
lost our convenor of this Committee, Mr. Thos. Davis, who 
has gone to take up a position at Windsor Mills. Mr. 
Davis will be missed by all who knew him, as a more faith- 
ful friend and true follower of the Lord Jesus Christ it 
would be hard to find. We wish Mr. Davis God speed in 
his new home. 

192 visits were made to the shops by the Secretary 
during the past twelve months, and men personally invited 
to attend our meetings and to visit the Association. 

Six Sunday Evening Teas have been held with an ave- 
rage attendance of 20. A lecture was given by Prof. 
Arnold, of Westmount, on “ Old Abbeys, Cathedrals and 
Castles of Scotland,’ An address was also given by the 
Rey. Mr. McKenzie, illustrated by limelight views. On 
New Year’s Day two hundred visitors were entertained, 
New Year’s evening being devoted to a concert. On Noy. 
12th, we held our Annual Concert, which netted $50.75. 

Our Women’s Auxiliary is still in a most flourishing 
condition. At the Annual Meeting Mrs. Mingie was again 
elected President. We are deeply indebted to the ladies 
for all they have done for our Association. After helping 
us financially and providing for each social occasion they 
enter upon their new year with a balance on hand of $43.76, 


60

FOR YOUNG MEN IN FOREIGN LANDS, 


Through the individual gifts of five members of the Association, 
men are sustained as Secretaries in India, and four in China, and 
one in Japan,—all of whom are engaged in work for the native 
young men of these non-Christian lands. 

The amount of $418.16 was contributed during the year, and for- 
warded to the International Committee for the support of Mr. David 
McConaughy’s work in India. 

R. F. Bell, A. Bruce, R. L. Charlton, J. G. Comrie, A. B. Dawson, 
W. Bell Dawson, A. W. Dewar, Rev. Thos. Everett, Dr. J. B. Hender- 
son, J. S. Hetherington, J. S. Hornibrook, Dr. P. C. Leslie, W. S. 
Leslie, H. A. Mackenzie, A. Mackellar, W. J. McCloy, N. L. Mason, 
C. L. Meyer, J. E. Millen, A. L. Mudge, J. Murphy, J. G. Readman, 
Geo. Rorke, D. W. Ross, J. W. Ross, A. E. Shaw, G. Sloan, W. Spark, 
J. C. Walker, G. C. Wells, H. J. Webber, J. Wilson, G. T. Woodley, 
and several friends.
